paper_title: CARE-3D: Reinforcement Learning for Evidence Grounded Agentic Reasoning in Situated 3D Scenes

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Situated 3D reasoning requires embodied agents to interpret objects, scene geometry, and viewpoint dependent spatial relations. Existing methods learn grounded interactions from supervised traces, but largely imitate prescribed evidence acquisition patterns rather than optimizing the support that the returned evidence provides for the correct answer. Moreover, outcome rewards provide limited credit for intermediate tool choices and may leave infrequent tools underexplored. An effective agent should instead adaptively decide what to ground, which tool to invoke, and how to assess the utility of returned evidence. To this end, this paper presents CARE-3D, a reinforcement post-training framework for adaptive grounded reasoning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on grounding instructions first establishes valid interactions, after which Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) optimizes the agent while keeping the 3D grounding module frozen. CARE-3D combines Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence for evidence sensitive credit assignment, and Group Coverage Sampling to preserve tool coverage. Experiments on MSQA and Beacon3D show consistent gains over SFT and GRPO using only answer and format rewards, especially in spatial reasoning and grounding answer coherence. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/xiaoqian-UQ/CARE-3D}{CARE-3D}.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Understanding and reasoning about 3D environments is fundamental capability for intelligent agents operating in the physical world. Effective 3D reasoning requires agents to recognize objects, interpret scene geometry, and connect language with their surroundings (Hong et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2024b). Situated 3D reasoning further requires these relations to be understood from specific observer position and orientation, making spatial meaning dependent on where the agent is located and facing (Ma et al., 2023; Linghu et al., Figure 1: Evidence-invariant predictions of the SFT policy. Predictions remain unchanged when the returned crop is replaced with fixed placeholder. The pillowbed association matches the scene in (a) but conflicts with it in (b), illustrating why answer correctness alone does not establish evidence use. 2024). This viewpoint aware capability supports embodied question answering, navigation, visionlanguage navigation, and grounded instruction following. It therefore represents an important step toward reliable and general purpose embodied intelligence. Existing 3D vision-language research has progressed from global scene representation toward explicit and situated grounding. Here, grounding refers to identifying the 3D scene objects referred by question or grounding query. Scene level models encode point clouds, object centric features, or multi-view observations to support semantic and spatial reasoning (Hong et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024b). Subsequent methods introduce explicit object references and 3D positional information to connect language reasoning with scene entities (Chen et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024a; Zhu et al., 2025). Situated approaches further incorporate the observers position and orientation (Yuan et al., 2025), while SceneCOT uses supervised grounding traces to acquire task specific scene evidence before answering (Linghu et al., 2026). These advances establish increasingly explicit and viewpoint aware interactions between language models and 3D environments. Despite this progress, supervised grounding Zero ( incorrect) Other answers (a) Generated answers (b) Probability mass 54.9 49.3 DKL = 0. 57.7 51.5 45.1 50.7 42.3 48.5 Full Masked Full Masked ) % ( t r 100 75 50 0 Figure 2: Evidence insensitive zero-count bias of the SFT policy on 71 MSQA counting errors with non-zero targets. Full retains the returned evidence, whereas Masked replaces it with fixed placeholder. The similar (a) zero-answer frequencies and (b) probability masses, together with the low mean divergence (DKL = 0.04), indicate limited sensitivity to grounding evidence. traces do not guarantee effective evidence use. Models may produce plausible answers despite incorrect grounding, revealing weak grounding answer coherence (Huang et al., 2025). Because each trace prescribes only one grounding call, it neither evaluates alternative tools nor verifies that the returned evidence supports the answer. Figure 1 illustrates this issue by comparing two evidence settings: Full, which retains the evidence returned by the grounding tool, and Masked, which replaces that evidence with fixed placeholder while keeping the question and grounding request unchanged. The SFT policy produces the same prediction in both settings, succeeding when its pillow-bed prior matches the scene but failing when the pillow is on sofa. Answer level rewards therefore cannot reliably distinguish evidence grounded reasoning from predictions driven by textual priors (Wang et al., 2026; Kong et al., 2026). Figure 2 further shows that, on 71 counting errors with non-zero ground truth answers, the policy predicts zero in nearly half the cases and changes little after evidence masking. Meanwhile, on-policy reinforcement learning may reduce sampling diversity, causing low frequency tools to disappear before their utility is evaluated (Yu et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2025). These limitations motivate evidence sensitive credit assignment and sustained grounding tool coverage. This paper presents CARE-3D, GRPO based reinforcement post-training framework that treats grounding as an adaptive information acquisition decision (Shao et al., 2024). CARE estimates evidence utility from the change in ground truth answer likelihood after masking the returned evidence. GCS adds loss masked rollouts for underrepresented tools, allowing evidence returned by these tools to participate in group relative comparison. Experiments on MSQA (Linghu et al., 2024) and Beacon3D (Huang et al., 2025) show consistent gains over SFT and answer and format only GRPO. The main contributions are: This paper formulates situated 3D grounding as adaptive evidence acquisition and presents CARE-3D, GRPO based reinforcement posttraining framework. CARE is introduced for evidence sensitive credit assignment and GCS for preserving grounding tool coverage during optimization. Experiments on MSQA and Beacon3D show consistent gains over SFT and GRPO using only answers and format rewards, with ablations validating both components.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: 3D Vision-Language Reasoning. 3D visionlanguage models use different scene representations to connect language reasoning with 3D environments. 3D-LLM aligns LLMs with multiview 3D features, while PointLLM directly instruction tunes language models over point cloud inputs (Hong et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024). LEO represents scenes through object centric tokens to support embodied perception, reasoning, and action (Huang et al., 2024b). Grounded 3D-LLM introduces referent tokens for linking generated language to scene objects, whereas Chat-Scene and LLaVA-3D incorporate object level scene representations and 3D positional information (Chen et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024a; Zhu et al., 2025). MSQA evaluates viewpoint dependent situated reasoning, while Beacon3D examines grounding answer coherence (Linghu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025). SceneCOT further constructs supervised grounding traces for stepwise evidence acquisition (Linghu et al., 2026). Unlike these approaches, CARE-3D reinforcement post trains grounding decisions according to the utility of the evidence they return. Grounded and Tool Augmented 3D Agents. Tool augmented 3D agents invoke external perception and geometry modules to acquire task specific Figure 3: Overview of CARE-3D. At inference, the agent selects grounding tool and reasons over its returned evidence. During post-training, GCS supplements free rollouts with underrepresented tools, while CARE computes Evidence Gain by contrasting ground truth answer likelihood under factual and evidence masked contexts. GRPO updates the agent using the resulting rewards. scene evidence. Earlier visual programming methods use LLM generated executable programs to compose off the shelf vision modules for training free visual reasoning (Gupta and Kembhavi, 2023). Think3D and RieMind coordinate tools such as object detection, depth estimation, and 3D reconstruction for spatial reasoning (Ropero et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). Skill-3D further learns scene aware skills from multi tool interaction trajectories (Li et al., 2026). These methods establish effective interfaces between language agents and 3D perception modules, but mainly learn tool use from constructed trajectories or aggregate task outcomes. CARE-3D focuses on directly attributing answer level utility to the evidence returned by each grounding call. Reinforcement Post-Training and Credit Assignment. Reinforcement post-training has extended from language reasoning to multimodal and tool using agents. Visual-RFT applies GRPO with task specific visual rewards, while DeepEyes and VToolR1 train VLMs to interleave reasoning with visual tool calls (Liu et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). For intermediate credit assignment, IGPO measures the increase in correct answer probability after each interaction, while InfoPO compares subsequent action distributions under factual and masked feedback (Wang et al., 2026; Kong et al., 2026). TACO assigns credit to individual tool calls using differential answer probes and routes outcome credit to the responsible interaction segments (Feng et al., 2026). These methods motivate deriving process credit from policy changes without an external reward model. CARE instead attributes the utility of multimodal evidence returned by 3D grounding call through counterfactual ground truth answer likelihood.

sections.title: 3 Problem Setup
sections.content: Situated 3D reasoning requires an agent to answer natural language question about 3D scene from specific observer viewpoint v, optionally accompanied by situation description s. The viewpoint is essential because spatial expressions such as left, behind, and two oclock depend on the observers position and orientation. Each task instance therefore consists of (S, v, s, q), while the agent initially receives the textual input = (s, q) and accesses the scene and viewpoint through 3D grounding module. Since the scene may contain many irrelevant objects and relations, the agent must identify question relevant scene entities and acquire appropriate grounded evidence before answering. Based on this evidence, the agent generates ˆy πθ( x, agrd, e), where πθ denotes the agent policy and denotes the ground truth answer. The objective is to produce an answer ˆy that is semantically consistent with and supported by both the 3D scene and the observer viewpoint.

sections.title: 4 Method
sections.content: CARE-3D optimizes how situated 3D reasoning agent acquires and uses scene evidence, as illustrated in Figure 3. The agent is first initialized through supervised grounding instruction tuning following SceneCOT (Linghu et al., 2026). The resulting grounding module is then frozen, while GRPO optimizes the agents grounding requests, tool use, reasoning, and answers. CARE-3D extends standard GRPO with Group Coverage Sampling (GCS) for diversified tool use and Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence (CARE) for evidence sensitive credit assignment. 4.1 Input Template Given the textual input = (s, q) defined in Section 3, the agent first generates grounding request with referential query and tool identifier. The selected tool returns evidence from the 3D scene. In the second turn, the agent reasons over this evidence and produces its final answer. Box 1 specifies the output format for both turns and refers to the returned evidence as an observation. Box 1: System Prompt You are precise 3D scene assistant. You should obtain one observation before answering. First assistant turn must contain exactly: <think_grd>evidence query</think_grd> tool from Tool list. The query line must be short noun phrase from the current question. Use concrete object, relation, viewpoint cue, or evidence phrase. Then output one tool tag from Tool list. 1. <list_obj_prob> Returns ranked object/category evidence with confidence scores. 2. <list_obj_loc_prob> Returns ranked object evidence with scene coordinate 3D centers, sizes, and prob. 3. <list_obj_loc_plr_prob> Returns ranked object evidence with viewer relative angle_deg, distance, and prob. 4. <highlight_obj> Returns visual evidence for queried object. Numeric interpretation: - prob: higher means more likely to match the query. - <list_obj_loc_prob>: [center_x, center_y, center_z, size_x, size_y, size_z]. Centers are scene coordinate positions. Sizes are extents along each axis. - <list_obj_loc_plr_prob>: object_name: angle_deg,distance ; prob: confidence. The first number is angle_deg, and the second number is distance. angle_deg is relative to viewer forward: 0 front, positive left, negative right, +/-180 behind. clock hour = round (((-angle_deg) mod 360) / 30), with 0 mapped to 12. Choose one tool from Tool list according to what returned evidence would make the answer best supported. After receiving the observation, answer: <reasoning> brief evidence based rationale </reasoning> <answer> final answer </answer> 4.2 Agentic Grounding Tools The grounding tool is selected from = {Prob, Cartesian, Polar, Crop}, whose four interfaces expose complementary outputs from the same grounding backend. Given referential query, Prob scores the candidate objects in the scene according to how well each matches the query, and returns their object identities or semantic categories ranked by grounding confidence. Cartesian returns the same ranked candidates together with the 3D center and spatial extent of each object in the global scene coordinate system, providing explicit information about object position and size. Polar transforms each candidates location into the observer centered coordinate system and reports its horizontal angle relative to the viewing direction and its distance from the observer. Crop retrieves visual region containing the grounded object and highlights its spatial extent, allowing the agent to inspect appearance information such as color, shape, and local surroundings. These interfaces respectively expose semantic matching, global 3D geometry, viewer relative geometry, and visual appearance. Different questions benefit from different evidence forms: object probabilities may suffice for existence reasoning, while clock direction questions require viewer relative spatial information. CARE-3D therefore treats both the grounding query and tool selection as policy decisions, allowing the agent to acquire task appropriate evidence rather than reproducing prescribed grounding action. 4.3 Agentic Workflow For an input x, the agent first samples structured grounding request agrd = (g, t), where is referential grounding query and is the selected grounding tool. Let Gϕ denote the 3D grounding module with parameters ϕ. The complete interaction is formulated as agrd = (g, t) πθ( x), = Gϕ(S, v, g, t), (r, y) πθ( x, agrd, e), (1) where is the evidence returned by the selected tool, is the reasoning trace, and is the generated answer. Following SceneCOT (Linghu et al., 2026), supervised grounding instruction tuning initializes the interaction protocol by teaching the agent to generate executable grounding requests and perform evidence conditioned reasoning, while jointly training the grounding module with annotated object targets. CARE-3D retains this procedure. Reinforcement post-training initializes both components from their supervised checkpoints, freezes the grounding module and vision-language backbone, and updates only the agents LoRA adapters. For input x, the i-th interaction rollout is τi = (agrd = (gi, ti) contains the grounding query gi and selected tool ti U, ei is , ei, ri, yi), where agrd the returned evidence, ri is the reasoning trace, and yi is the final answer. 4.4 Diversified Tool Use in Group Rollouts Group based reinforcement learning may increasingly concentrate on frequently sampled behaviors, reducing policy entropy and rollout diversity (Yu et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2025). In CARE-3D, this tendency can cause low frequency grounding tools to disappear from rollout group before their utility has been adequately evaluated. An absent tool receives no reward based comparison, and CARE cannot evaluate the evidence that it might have returned. For each training prompt x, Group Coverage Sampling (GCS) first samples six free on-policy rollouts, denoted by Tfree(x). Let valid free (x) denote the subset with valid grounding calls. The coverage count for each tool is cx(u) = (cid:88) I[ti = u]. (2) τiT valid free (x) Malformed calls and unsupported tool identifiers are excluded from the counts. GCS selects the two distinct tools with the lowest counts, including tools with zero occurrences, and generates one coverage rollout for each. The resulting GRPO group contains eight rollouts: six free rollouts and two coverage rollouts. In each coverage rollout, GCS supplies the tool identifier. The policy generates the grounding query, reasoning trace, and final answer, and the grounding module returns evidence using the supplied tool. The policy loss masks the supplied tool identifier and the returned evidence. The remaining policy-generated tokens are optimized with GRPO. Free and coverage rollouts use the same reward function and participate in the same group-relative advantage computation. Unlike dynamic sampling in DAPO (Yu et al., 2025), which discards groups with uniform outcome rewards, GCS retains all free rollouts and supplements them with underrepresented tools. It changes only rollout group construction, introduces no additional reward, and is disabled during evaluation. Further details are provided in Appendix A.5. 4.5 Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence Final answer rewards do not reveal whether grounding request returns useful evidence. correct answer may arise from language priors despite irrelevant evidence, while useful evidence may receive no credit if later reasoning fails. Fixed tool bonuses cannot resolve this ambiguity because they reward tool invocation rather than the utility of its returned evidence. Inspired by likelihood based intermediate credit assignment (Wang et al., 2026; Kong et al., 2026), CARE measures how much the returned evidence supports the ground truth answer. CARE constructs counterfactual context by replacing ei with fixed evidence masked placeholder m(ei), while keeping the input and grounding request unchanged. For rollout τi, let = (y 1, . . . , i CARE deliberately excludes the sampled reasoning trace from these scoring contexts. Its purpose is to measure how strongly the returned evidence itself supports the ground truth answer, rather than to evaluate particular sampled reasoning trajectory. Because reasoning is generated after the evidence is returned, it is an evidence dependent intermediate variable and may already encode the predicted conclusion. Regenerating reasoning under the two contexts would introduce an additional source of variation, whereas reusing the factual reasoning could preserve answer information after the evidence is masked and thereby obscure its contribution. CARE therefore scores the same ground truth answer tokens directly under two matched pre-reasoning contexts that differ only in the availability of returned evidence. The sigmoid maps this standardized score to bounded CARE reward in (0, 1), making it compatible with the other reward components. CARE assigns credit to evidence utility rather than merely to tool use. For example, for question asking which object is located at the agents two oclock, polar evidence receives higher credit when it substantially increases the likelihood of the target object. Evidence whose removal produces little likelihood change receives lower credit. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: CARE-3D is reinforcement post-training framework for evidence grounded situated 3D reasoning. CARE assigns credit to returned evidence, whereas GCS preserves tool coverage during optimization. Across MSQA and Beacon3D, their combination outperforms SFT and answer and format GRPO, particularly in spatial reasoning and grounding answer coherence. These findings highlight the importance of jointly optimizing evidence acquisition and use for reliable situated 3D reasoning.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: CARE-3D currently performs single grounding action per question and therefore does not support iterative query refinement or multi tool composition. Future work could extend the framework to multi step grounding, allowing the agent to refine unsuccessful requests and combine complementary evidence. CARE estimates evidence utility by masking returned evidence and scoring the ground truth answer. This counterfactual may introduce distribution shift, while likelihood scores can be affected by answer phrasing. Future work may explore in distribution counterfactuals, semantically normalized scoring, and reasoning aware credit assignment. CARE also increases training time computation by evaluating factual and evidence masked contexts, although it introduces no additional inference time cost. Potential risks. Although CARE-3D is designed for research, incorrect grounding or spatial reasoning could lead to unsafe behavior if deployed in embodied systems. Its outputs should therefore not be used in safety-critical settings without human oversight and additional validation.

A Additional Experimental and
Implementation Details
sections.content: A.1 Experimental Setup Datasets. Following prior situated 3D reasoning studies (Linghu et al., 2024, 2026; Huang et al., 2025), CARE-3D is evaluated on the widely used MSQA and Beacon3D benchmarks. MSQA is large scale situated 3D question answering benchmark constructed from ScanNet, 3RScan, and ARKitScenes (Dai et al., 2017; Wald et al., 2019; Dehghan et al., 2021). Each question is associated with 3D scene and specific observer viewpoint, requiring semantic, geometric, and egocentric reasoning. Following SceneCOT, performance is reported for six question categories: counting, existence, attribute/description, spatial/referential, navigation, and others. Beacon3D evaluates 3D grounding, question answering, and grounding answer coherence using per case and object level metrics. Supervised finetuning is performed using interaction traces derived from MSQA and GQA3D (Linghu et al., 2026), whereas reinforcement post-training is conducted only on the MSQA training split. Beacon3D is used exclusively for evaluation. Following SceneCOT-185K, the supervised data comprise 145.6K MSQA-based situated reasoning traces and 40K GQA3D-based object-centric traces. Reinforcement post-training uses only the MSQA training split, while evaluation follows the official MSQA and Beacon3D evaluation sets. MSQA contains 10,891 sets comprising 34,357 samples with evidence augmentation. Within each group, samples share the scene, question, and target but differ in observer pose, with pose-consistent answers. Our SFT baseline retains the corresponding pose-augmented training examples. Baselines. The evaluation compares CARE-3D with representative multimodal and 3D visionlanguage methods, including GPT-4o, SplatTalk, LEO, MSR3D, Chat-Scene, and SceneCOT (OpenAI, 2024; Thai et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2024b; Linghu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024a; Linghu et al., 2026). These baselines cover closed source multimodal models, general purpose 3D agents, situated reasoning models, and methods based on object centric or 3D Gaussian scene representations. SceneCOT is the closest grounded reasoning baseline and learns stepwise grounding interactions from supervised traces. Two controlled training baselines are further included. The SFT baseline corresponds to the policy trained solely with supervised grounding traces. The Answer+Format baseline applies GRPO with only answer and format rewards. It excludes CARE and GCS. Other component combinations are examined in the ablation study. Evaluation Metrics. Following the official evaluation protocols, GPT-Score is used to measure the semantic correctness of generated answers. For MSQA, performance is reported for six reasoning categories: counting, existence, attribute/description, spatial/referential, navigation, and others. The overall score is computed over all evaluation questions. For Beacon3D, Case averages the scores of individual question answer pairs, while Obj. requires all questions associated with the same target object to be answered correctly. The latter provides stricter measure of grounding answer coherence. All metrics are reported on 0-100 scale, and higher values indicate better performance. The LLM judge used as the answer reward during reinforcement post-training is not used for final evaluation. Implementation. CARE-3D uses Qwen3-VL4B-Instruct as the primary vision-language agent, adapted with LoRA of rank 16 and scaling factor 32. The agent and 3D grounding module are first jointly optimized using supervised interaction traces. Reinforcement post-training starts from the resulting SFT checkpoint, with the grounding module and vision-language backbone frozen and only the agents LoRA parameters updated. GRPO optimization is conducted on MSQA for 600 steps, using 24 prompts and 192 sampled trajectories per step. Each GRPO group contains six free rollouts and two GCS coverage rollouts. The answer reward is computed using an LLM judge. A.2 Training Configurations Supervised fine-tuning jointly optimizes the agent and 3D grounding module using supervised demonstrations. GRPO reinforcement post-training starts from the resulting SFT checkpoint, freezes the grounding module and vision-language backbone, and updates only the agents LoRA parameters. No separate grounder only refinement is performed. Tables 7 and 8 summarize the optimization settings for supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement posttraining, respectively. LoRA configuration. Supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement post-training use the same LoRA architecture, with rank = 16, scaling parameter α = 32, and an effective scaling ratio of α/r = 2. LoRA is applied to the q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, and down_proj modules. During Supervised fine-tuning, the agent LoRA parameters and all trainable components of the grounding module share single AdamW parameter group and therefore use the same learning rate of 2 105. Supervised fine-tuning batch construction. Supervised fine-tuning uses four training samples per GPU, two GPUs, and five gradient accumulation steps, resulting in an effective global batch size of 4 2 5 = 40 samples per optimizer update. The maximum input context length is 1,024 tokens, and the maximum supervised output length is 768 tokens. GRPO batch construction. Batch parameters in GRPO operate at different granularities: the training batch size counts prompts, whereas actor updates operate on trajectories. Each GRPO step processes 24 prompts, and each prompt yields group of = 8 trajectories (six free on-policy Each GRPO step thus contains 192/96 = 2 actor mini batches; with one PPO epoch, 600 GRPO steps correspond to approximately 1,200 actor optimizer updates, and the complete run samples 600 24 8 = 115,200 training trajectories. GRPO hyperparameters. The GRPO clipping parameter is set to ε = 0.2 such that the policy ratio is clipped to [1 ε, 1 + ε] = [0.8, 1.2], giving symmetric lower and upper clipping ranges of 0.2. The coefficient of the KL regularization term in Equation 8 is β = 0.02. KL divergence is estimated using low variance KL estimator and is added directly to the actor loss; it is not incorporated into the scalar rollout reward. CARE-3D uses one PPO epoch per GRPO step, an entropy coefficient of zero, and maximum gradient norm of 1.0. Rollout generation. Training rollouts are sampled with temperature 0.7, top-p = 0.9, and no topk truncation. The maximum prompt length is 2,048 tokens, and the complete single grounding interaction has total response budget of 1,700 tokens. Validation uses greedy decoding with temperature zero, top-p = 1.0, and one generated response per question. Additional thresholding or binarization is not applied. The complete judge prompt is provided in Appendix B. This training time judge is separate from the GPT-Score evaluator used for final benchmark evaluation. Sensitivity to the answer reward judge. We examine the sensitivity of CARE-3D to the language model used to compute the answer reward. In addition to the default Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite judge, we use Qwen3-4B and GPT-5.6 Luna, while keeping all other training settings and the final benchmark evaluator fixed. Table 10 shows score differences of at most 0.7, 0.6, and 0.4 points on MSQA Overall, Beacon3D Case, and Beacon3D Obj., respectively. All variants use the same final benchmark evaluator. CARE reward. The CARE reward is computed according to Equation 4. The factual and evidence masked likelihoods are evaluated using the fixed rollout policy πθ. The resulting reward lies in (0, 1) and is assigned constant weight of wCARE = 0.2 throughout reinforcement post-training. Reward schedule and controlled variants. For the first 200 optimization steps, the format and answer weights are set to 1.2 and 0.8, respectively. They are switched to 0.8 and 1.2 for the remaining 400 steps. The reward schedule and answer judge are shared across all reinforcement post-training variants. Variants without CARE set wCARE = 0, whereas GCS changes only rollout group construction and introduces no additional reward. A.4 CARE Implementation CARE follows Equations 3 and 4. It is computed after rollout generation and before group relative advantage estimation. Only executable rollouts are scored. Likelihood computation. The policy used to generate the rollouts also serves as the CARE scoring policy. It is placed in evaluation mode and remains fixed during reward computation. For each factual or evidence masked context, CARE computes the mean log likelihood over the non padding ground truth answer tokens. Prompt tokens, returned evidence, and padding tokens are excluded from this average. The two contexts score exactly the same ground truth answer tokens, and no gradient is propagated through either likelihood computation. Normalization and GCS integration. Evidence Gains are normalized across the executable rollouts associated with the same question. The normalization constant is set to ϵ = 106 for numerical stability. The same scoring procedure is applied to free and GCS coverage rollouts. For coverage rollout, the tool identifier inserted by GCS remains in both scoring contexts but is excluded from the policy loss. CARE therefore evaluates the returned evidence without treating the inserted tool identifier as supervised target. A.5 GCS Implementation Group Coverage Sampling (GCS) is applied independently to each training prompt during reinforcement post-training. The policy first samples six free on-policy rollouts using the rollout generation settings reported in Appendix A.2. The grounding tool identifier in each valid rollout is parsed, and the occurrence count of each tool in {Prob, Cartesian, Polar, Crop} is recorded. Malformed calls and unsupported tool identifiers do not increase the count of any valid tool. The two tools with the lowest occurrence counts are selected for coverage sampling. One intervened rollout is generated for each selected tool, producing group of eight rollouts: six free rollouts and two intervened coverage rollouts. In coverage rollout, GCS supplies only the tool identifier. The grounding query, reasoning trace, and final answer remain generated by the current policy, and the grounding module returns evidence normally using the supplied tool. token level loss mask excludes each GCS supplied tool identifier from the policy loss. Returned tool evidence is also excluded because it is generated by the grounding module rather than the policy. All remaining policy generated tokens participate normally in GRPO optimization. Free and coverage rollouts use the same reward function, CARE computation, and group relative advantage estimation. GCS therefore changes the composition of the rollout group without introducing an additional reward or training the policy to imitate externally selected tools. GCS is enabled only during reinforcement posttraining and is disabled during evaluation, where the policy selects grounding tools without GCS coverage sampling. The default number of coverage rollouts is set to two. The effect of varying the number of coverage is reported in Table 3. A.6 Error Analysis and Evidence Interventions correct answer alone does not establish appropriate evidence use. We therefore conduct error-type and evidence-intervention analyses on 1,369 validation samples to compare the SFT and CARE-3D policies. Error-type analysis. We examine two diagnostic error types: incorrect grounding and misinterpretation of returned evidence. As shown in Table 11, CARE-3D improves answer accuracy from 49.7% to 56.8%, while reducing incorrect grounding from 37.3% to 29.0% and misinterpreted evidence from 9.8% to 4.5%. These results suggest improvements in both evidence acquisition and interpretation. Acc. sections.title: B Prompts
sections.content: This section presents the prompts used for LLM based answer evaluation. In the implementation prompts, observation refers to the grounded evidence returned by the selected tool. Box 2: Training Time Answer Judge Prompt Score open-ended answers from 1 to 5 based on semantic accuracy, completeness, and relevance to the ground truth. Please follow the following rules: - Judge semantic correctness, not exact wording. - Accept synonyms, paraphrases, singular/plural changes, harmless extra details, and reasonable specificity differences. - If the prediction is more general than the ground truth but captures the main answer, give partial credit. - For object lists, do not require every item unless the question asks for all objects. - For spatial or navigation answers, minor direction or distance errors should receive partial credit. - Only give Score 1 when the answer is clearly wrong, contradicts the ground truth, is irrelevant, or refuses to answer when the ground truth provides an answer.

sections.title: C Qualitative Examples
sections.content: This section presents qualitative comparisons between the SFT policy and the CARE-3D policy across three representative reasoning categories: counting, existence, and navigation. Each example compares the grounding request, selected tool, returned scene evidence, and final prediction produced by the two policies. These cases illustrate how reinforcement post-training enables CARE3D to select more task appropriate grounding tools and make better use of the returned evidence. In particular, CARE-3D exhibits stronger grounding answer coherence, producing answers that are more consistently supported by the acquired visual and spatial information. Figure 6: Qualitative comparison on counting question. CARE-3D uses more specific grounding query to retrieve sufficient object evidence and produce the correct count. Figure 7: Qualitative comparison on an existence question. CARE-3D selects viewer relative polar evidence that directly supports the specified clock direction. Figure 8: Qualitative comparison on navigation question. CARE-3D retrieves viewer relative direction and distance evidence to generate grounded navigation instruction.
